explanations: terra: The Fire's fuel is people and stones, bringing heated stone and human flesh together as the source-section qahīra and qahr senses separately do; the culinary bridge is indirect because the stones here are fuel.
terra: Adam and his wife are told to dwell in the Garden and eat freely and plentifully, an indirect parallel to the no-hunger security recalled in the section through 20:118.

luna: The section brings together forenoon warmth and food; here God shades Israel with clouds and provides manna and quail to eat, joining bodily cover and a meal in one provision scene. | terra: Cloud shade and the descent of manna and quails place shelter from exposure and good food in one divine gift, the same conjunction made explicit in 20:118-119.
terra: The people exchange manna and quails for a list of ordinary plant foods, and humiliation and poverty follow; the ayah makes choice of food and a state of deprivation part of one scene.
terra: The command concerning orphans says reform is best and, if households are mixed, the orphans are brothers; it replaces dominating isolation with protected shared life.

luna: The section joins food and heat; this parable's garden of fruit is struck by a fiery whirlwind («إِعْصَارٌ فِيهِ نَارٌ فَاحْتَرَقَتْ»), showing heat destroying provision. | terra: A lush, fruitful garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind and burned; it supplies the destructive reversal behind the source-section qily made by burning living plants.

luna: The section's B004 cooked-meat and B002 fire-on-flesh branches meet a different fire scene: the demanded offering is one «تَأْكُلُهُ النَّارُ», a ritual sign rather than a meal. | terra: The demanded sign is a sacrificial offering consumed by fire, a direct meeting of food or flesh with the consuming fire disclosed by the section's qaly and qahr senses.

luna: The section forbids overpowering the orphan; this command identifies consuming or exchanging an orphan's property as a concrete form of the prohibited harm. | terra: The prohibition on consuming an orphan's property into one's own wealth turns predatory “eating” into a form of the qahr the section forbids.

terra: Guardians are forbidden to consume orphan property wastefully; the rich must abstain and a poor guardian may take only fairly, setting a precise boundary where eating, poverty, and orphan care meet.
terra: When orphans and needy people attend an estate division, the heirs are told to provide for them from it and speak kindly, joining material nourishment to non-oppressive treatment.

luna: The section sets a meal against malnutrition and forbids overpowering an orphan; this verse says unjustly consuming orphans' wealth is «يَأْكُلُونَ فِي بُطُونِهِمْ نَارًا», a specific reversal where food becomes fire. | terra: Those who consume an orphan's property are said to eat fire into their bellies; this single ayah fuses the section's orphan, eating, oppression, and fire images.

luna: B002's qahr describes fire acting on meat; here the fire cooks skins («نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُمْ») and they are replaced, making the harmful bodily force explicit. | terra: Hell's skins repeatedly become cooked through, نَضِجَتْ جُلُودُهُمْ; the source-section definition of qaly likewise says meat is roasted until it is made ناضج, so the dictionary cooking sense becomes a Quranic bodily scene.
terra: The command to stand for justice for orphans supplies the positive social relation opposite the qahr forbidden toward the orphan in the section.
terra: Feeding ten poor people must come from the average food one feeds one's own family, giving a concrete standard of adequate nourishment against the section's bad-feeding sense.
luna: The section's B003 meal sense evokes a table; the disciples ask Jesus for «مَائِدَةً مِّنَ السَّمَاءِ», a concrete table scene of requested provision.
luna: The next ayah says the disciples want to eat from the table and have their hearts reassured; it specifies the table's food and purpose.
luna: Jesus prays that the table be a feast for the first and last of them and a sign; this ayah makes the requested table a shared meal and gift.
luna: God answers that He will send the table down, then warns of punishment for disbelief; this completes the provision scene with its stated boundary.
terra: God alone is ٱلْقَاهِرُ فَوْقَ عِبَادِهِ; divine mastery over all servants marks the boundary against a human being's forbidden qahr of an orphan.
terra: Again naming God ٱلْقَاهِرُ above His servants in a context of guardianship and death distinguishes absolute divine qahr from human abuse of the unprotected.

luna: The section's qahr line sets a boundary on harm to the orphan; this ayah specifies that boundary for the orphan's property, which must not be approached except in the best way until maturity. | terra: Approaching orphan property is barred except in the best manner until maturity, giving a concrete boundary against overpowering the vulnerable orphan.
terra: Eating from the forbidden tree makes Adam and his wife's nakedness appear, paralleling the food-and-exposure consequences that 20:117-119 frame as loss of Garden security.
terra: The people of the towns feel secure from punishment arriving ضُحًى while they play; the same forenoon that suggests warmth and a meal can also be the exposed hour of sudden judgment.
terra: Pharaoh promises to kill sons and declares وَإِنَّا فَوْقَهُمْ قَٰهِرُونَ; this is the same qahr as human domination, exemplifying the cruelty excluded by the command concerning the orphan.

luna: This repeated wilderness scene pairs cloud shade with manna and quail and the command to eat from God's provision; it gives another specific meeting of protection and food. | terra: This parallel wilderness scene again combines cloud shade with manna and quails, then commands the people to eat the good things provided.

luna: The section links needy «عَائِلًا» and enrichment with a B004 branch about poor nourishment; here «عَيْلَةٍ» (want) is answered by «يُغْنِكُمُ اللَّهُ», a close root-and-provision parallel. | terra: عَيْلَةً is the same poverty root as the section's عَائِلًا, and يُغْنِيكُمُ ٱللَّهُ repeats the movement from feared poverty to God's enrichment found in 93:8.
terra: Hoarded metal is heated in Hell and used to brand foreheads, sides, and backs, a direct Quranic instance of fire taking hold of bodily flesh.
terra: Those who refuse to march cite the heat, and the reply says Hell's fire is hotter; worldly solar heat and punitive fire are directly measured against each other.

luna: The B004 dictionary branch for ق ل ي describes meat roasted until cooked; Abraham's visitors are served «عِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ», a direct cooked-meat scene beside the section's lexicon dish. | terra: Abraham brings a roasted calf, عِجْلٍ حَنِيذٍ, a direct Quranic scene for the source-section qaly sense of cooking meat over heat until done.
luna: After the roasted calf in 11:69, the visitors' hands «لَا تَصِلُ إِلَيْهِ»; this ayah adds Abraham's alarm at an untouched meal, a distinct response within the cooked-meat scene.

terra: The prisoner's dream of carrying bread from which birds eat preserves flour transformed into food, indirectly recalling the flour added to the source-section qahīra; the ayah names bread rather than flour or heat.
terra: Joseph contrasts scattered lords with Allah, ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ; in prison, the title locates ultimate domination in the one God rather than human masters.
terra: After denying that powerless partners create as God creates, the ayah names Him ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ; this cosmic qahr sets a limit on the human domination forbidden in the section.
terra: The inhabitant of Hell is given foul fluid to drink, turning served provision into bodily harm rather than relief from thirst.
terra: He tries to gulp the drink but can scarcely swallow it, and death comes from every side without ending him; this completes the anti-nourishing drink scene of 14:16.

luna: The section's B006 qily is ash made by burning plants and used to wash clothes; this verse uses wind-scattered ash («رَمَادٍ») as an image of vanished deeds. The link is only the specific fire-made residue, not a shared cleansing sense. | terra: The deeds of disbelievers are likened to ashes blown violently on a stormy day; the ayah supplies the ash that remains after the source-section qily plants are burned.
terra: All creatures emerge before ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ on the transformed earth, making qahr universal divine sovereignty rather than license to crush a vulnerable person.
terra: Garments of pitch and fire covering faces give another precise bodily surface upon which fire acts, close to the section's fire-seizing-flesh expression.
terra: Livestock provide warmth and other benefits and are also eaten from, placing protection from cold beside the animal food behind the section's heated meat and milk dishes.
terra: لَبَنًا خَالِصًا, pure palatable milk, is the exact foodstuff from which the source-section qahīra is made before hot stones and flour are added.

luna: The section begins with exposure to sun and names B006 plant ash used to wash garments; here garments «تَقِيكُمُ الْحَرَّ» protect people from heat, linking clothing to the same bodily exposure. | terra: God provides shade, shelters, and garments that protect from heat, سَرَابِيلَ تَقِيكُمُ ٱلْحَرَّ, a direct answer to the sun exposure latent in ḍuḥā.

luna: This repeated property command makes the orphan-protection in the section concrete: do not approach the orphan's wealth except in the best manner until maturity. | terra: This repeated prohibition protects orphan property until maturity and requires fulfillment of covenant, another specific limit on the human power named by qahr.
terra: The rising sun inclines away from the cave and the setting sun passes its occupants by, making their preservation partly a scene of controlled solar exposure.

luna: The section's qahr branch describes fire taking meat; here water like molten metal «يَشْوِي الْوُجُوهَ», a specific reversal from prepared food to scalding harm. | terra: The drink of the wrongdoers is like molten metal and scalds faces; a served drink becomes the agent of the section's fire-on-flesh image.
terra: Rain-fed vegetation becomes dry debris scattered by wind, an indirect parallel to the source-section wet plants becoming ash and to Quranic windblown ash; the ayah contains no fire.

luna: B003 says «الضحاء» can name «الغداء»; Musa asks for «غَدَاءَنَا» after travel fatigue. This gives the section's forenoon-meal sense a concrete scene of need and provision. | terra: Moses says آتِنَا غَدَآءَنَا, “bring our morning meal”; الغداء is precisely the source-section dictionary gloss used to disclose a meal inside ḍuḥā.
terra: At the eastern limit the sun rises upon people for whom no screen from it was made; this is the Quran's most concrete scene of unshielded solar exposure.
terra: The people of the Garden receive their provision morning and evening; the morning period thus carries a table in the Quran as the source dictionary says of ḍuḥā.

luna: The section names duha as the forenoon time; at the contest with Pharaoh, the people are gathered «ضُحًى», making that named daylight hour a public scene. | terra: Moses fixes the contest for the festival day when people are gathered ضُحًى; it preserves the root's public forenoon-time sense alongside the heat and meal senses developed by the section.

luna: Allah warns Adam not to be expelled from the Garden or become wretched; neighboring 20:118–119 name hunger and exposure to sun as what the Garden assurance prevents. | terra: This warning identifies the enemy who would expel Adam and his wife from the Garden and thereby expose Adam to hardship; 20:118-119 specify that hardship as hunger, thirst, nakedness, and sun.

luna: The section's meal sense meets the Garden assurance «أَلَّا تَجُوعَ»; its own contribution is freedom from hunger, while neighboring 20:119 adds freedom from thirst and sun exposure. | terra: The Garden guarantee begins with freedom from hunger and nakedness; together with 20:119 it binds adequate food to shelter from exposure, the same pairing the section hears in the forenoon.

luna: The section's B002 root ض ح و names exposure to sun; Adam's assurance uses «تَضْحَىٰ» for the heat he will avoid in the Garden. The shared divine promise makes the source's warmth explicitly a boundary of bodily ease. | terra: The same root becomes direct sun exposure in وَلَا تَضْحَىٰ: Adam is promised freedom from thirst and the sun's heat, making explicit the heat latent in the section's forenoon.
terra: Adam and his wife eat from the tree and their nakedness appears; this enacts the loss of the food-and-clothing security promised in 20:118 after the enemy warning of 20:117.

luna: The people command «حَرِّقُوهُ» against Abraham; this makes fire an act of human harm, the boundary reversed when the next ayah makes it cool and safe. | terra: Abraham's opponents explicitly command one another to burn him; this supplies the intended fire-on-flesh action that God's command in 21:69 reverses.

luna: Where 21:68 commands Abraham's burning, «كُونِي بَرْدًا وَسَلَامًا» reverses fire's harm in this ayah; it marks a boundary to the section's qahr image of fire overcoming flesh. | terra: God commands the intended burning fire to become coolness and safety for Abraham, the clearest reversal of the section's image of fire taking flesh.

terra: Garments of fire and boiling liquid poured over heads begin the flesh-and-fire scene whose bodily effect 22:20 states, closely realizing the section's culinary senses of qaly and qahr as punishment.

luna: The section's qahr image is fire overpowering flesh; here boiling water melts what is in bellies and skins («مَا فِي بُطُونِهِمْ وَالْجُلُودُ»), a specific bodily reversal. | terra: Boiling liquid melts what is in bellies and the skins, directly corresponding to the source-section qahr image in which fire takes meat and its moisture runs out.

luna: The section turns the forenoon meal toward hunger; this rite explicitly pairs eating from the livestock offering with feeding «الْبَائِسَ الْفَقِيرَ». | terra: People are told to eat from the sacrificial livestock and feed the afflicted poor, joining the source-section meat meal to relief of bad nourishment.

luna: B004 names a qalya from camel meat and livers; here sacrificial camels become food to eat and share with the contented and needy («وَأَطْعِمُوا الْقَانِعَ وَالْمُعْتَرَّ»), joining the cooked-meat sense to provision. | terra: The sacrificial camels are eaten from and used to feed both the contented and the petitioner; this directly meets the source-section qaliyya made from camel meat and its table set against want.

luna: After 22:36's camel meat is eaten and shared, this ayah says its meat and blood do not reach God, but piety does; it marks the limit of the section's physical cooking image. | terra: After the command to eat camel meat and feed others, this ayah states that neither flesh nor blood reaches God but piety does, fixing the meal's ethical purpose rather than its cooking alone.

luna: The section's dictionary branches name a camel-meat dish and a heated-milk dish; this verse puts drink from livestock beside eating from them, linking both ingredients to provided nourishment. | terra: One ayah places drinking what is in livestock's bellies beside eating from the animals; it gathers the milk base of qahīra and the meat base of qaliyya in a single provision scene.
luna: The section pairs sun-light with cooking fire; this lamp image says its oil nearly shines «وَلَوْ لَمْ تَمْسَسْهُ نَارٌ», sharply separating illumination from flame.

luna: The section joins forenoon sunlight to heat; this passage describes the sun as the guide to an extended shadow, adding the sun's changing shade as a specific counterpoint to exposure. | terra: God extends shade and makes the sun its indicator, showing sun and shade as a measured relation rather than treating forenoon heat in isolation.
terra: God then draws the extended shade in gradually, making relief from sun a bestowed and measured condition.
terra: Moses sees a fire and hopes to bring his family a burning brand so that they may warm themselves, presenting fire as useful bodily warmth rather than bodily destruction.
terra: This repeated scene has Moses sight fire and seek a firebrand so that his family may warm themselves, directly connecting seen fire with relief from cold.

luna: In a repeated account of Abraham's trial, the people choose killing or burning, but Allah saves him from fire; this adds another specific reversal of fire's overpowering force. | terra: Abraham's people propose killing or burning him, but God saves him from the fire in the same ayah; the fire-to-flesh action is explicitly attempted and excluded.

luna: The section insists duha is heat as well as light; «الظِّلُّ» and «الْحَرُورُ» are explicitly set apart, making shade and scorching heat the image's climatic boundary. | terra: وَلَا ٱلظِّلُّ وَلَا ٱلْحَرُورُ sets shade and scorching heat as non-equivalent opposites, clarifying the boundary between shelter and the exposure sensed in ḍuḥā.
terra: The revived earth brings out grain “from which they eat,” supplying both the qaly dictionary's grain object and its purpose as nourishment.
terra: The disbelievers answer a command to spend by asking why they should feed someone God could feed; it is an explicit refusal of the provision-table the section makes visible.
terra: God subjects livestock to people so that some carry them and some are eaten, another direct animal-food counterpart to the source-section qaliyya.
terra: Livestock also yield benefits and drinks, joining the milk side of the source-section qahīra to the meat eaten in 36:72.
terra: God makes fire for people from the green tree, مِنَ ٱلشَّجَرِ ٱلْأَخْضَرِ نَارًا; this closely matches the source-section qily made by burning green plants.
terra: The passage explicitly asks whether Garden hospitality or the tree of zaqqum is the better welcome, framing Hell's burning food as an anti-table.
terra: The food-tree grows from the bottom of Hell, physically joining vegetation and fire as the source-section qily image does.

luna: Against the section's meal and cooked-meat lexicon, this passage says the people of the Tree of Zaqqum fill their bellies from it («فَمَالِئُونَ مِنْهَا الْبُطُونَ»), turning eating into torment. | terra: The condemned eat from the tree and fill their bellies, making its status as punitive nourishment concrete.

luna: The next ayah completes 37:66's meal with «شَوْبًا مِّنْ حَمِيمٍ»; it makes the hot, harmful accompaniment explicit against the section's nourishing table. | terra: A mixture of boiling water follows the zaqqum meal, joining eating and scalding liquid as in the section's hot-food senses.
luna: After the Zaqqum and hot drink in 37:66–67, this ayah says their return is to the blazing fire; it completes the harmful-meal scene.

luna: In another telling of Abraham's trial, his people say «فَأَلْقُوهُ فِي الْجَحِيمِ»; this is fire imposed as violence, unlike the section's cooking image. | terra: Abraham's people build a structure and cast him into the blazing fire, another concrete attempt to let fire take a human body that divine rescue defeats.
luna: This neighbor says their plot made them «الْأَسْفَلِينَ»; it completes the attempted burning in 37:97 with the reversal of the burners' power.
terra: The messenger declares no deity but Allah, ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ; the divine title provides the theological boundary around the section's prohibition of human qahr.
terra: In rejecting divine offspring, the ayah closes with ٱلْوَٰحِدُ ٱلْقَهَّارُ, assigning unconstrained qahr to God alone.
terra: Water produces varied crops that then yellow and become broken residue, a repeated plant-to-residue transformation related indirectly to the source-section qily ash, without explicit burning.
terra: On the day all are exposed, sovereignty belongs to Allah, ٱلْوَٰحِدِ ٱلْقَهَّارِ; universal divine qahr contrasts with domination of an orphan in ordinary human life.
terra: Pharaoh's people are exposed to the Fire morning and evening; the recurring morning that can announce a meal becomes recurring exposure to flame.
terra: The condemned are dragged through boiling water and then burned in the Fire, directly staging heated liquid followed by fire acting upon bodies.
terra: God made livestock so that people ride some and eat from some; the eating of large livestock directly recalls the source-section camel-meat dish.
terra: The tree of zaqqum is introduced as food before its heat effect is described, beginning an inverted meal that culminates in boiling inside the eater.

luna: The section's cooking words make food audible; this passage names Zaqqum «طَعَامُ الْأَثِيمِ», the food of the sinner, setting an infernal meal against the shared meal. | terra: Calling zaqqum “the food of the sinner” fixes the plant as a meal rather than generic fire imagery.

luna: Continuing 44:44, the food «يَغْلِي فِي الْبُطُونِ» like molten metal; this is cooking's bodily harm rather than nourishment. | terra: That food is like molten substance in the bellies, moving the cooking heat inside flesh in a way that echoes the section's qaly and qahr definitions.

luna: The next ayah sharpens 44:45's boiling comparison with «كَغَلْيِ الْحَمِيمِ», a hot-water image that reverses the section's prepared food. | terra: It boils like boiling water, كَغَلْىِ ٱلْحَمِيمِ, directly matching the source-section qahīra's boiling-food scene while reversing nourishment into punishment.
terra: Boiling water is poured over the condemned person's head, continuing 44:43-46's meal that boils inside the belly with an external cooking-like action upon the body.

luna: The section's B003 qahira is milk heated with stones; this Garden description places milk «لَمْ يَتَغَيَّرْ طَعْمُهُ» beside boiling water, marking a boundary between sustaining milk and scorching liquid. | terra: One ayah contrasts Garden rivers of milk whose taste never changes with boiling water that cuts intestines; it places the source-section qahīra's pure milk and boiling bodily harm on opposite sides of the final boundary.

luna: The section's B004 branch names a meat dish; Abraham quietly brings «عِجْلٍ سَمِينٍ» to his guests, a distinct meal scene though this ayah does not say it is roasted. | terra: Abraham goes quietly to his household and returns with a fat calf, opening the parallel meal scene to the roasted calf of 11:69.

luna: This continuation of 51:26 says Abraham places the calf before them and invites them to eat («أَلَا تَأْكُلُونَ»), completing the guest-meal scene. | terra: He places the calf before his guests and asks why they do not eat, making the cooked animal an offered table rather than merely an object.

luna: The section's B004 dictionary develops cooked meat as food; this Garden provision includes «لَحْمٍ مِّمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ», putting meat in a scene of desired sustenance, without specifying cooking.
terra: The guilty circulate between Hell and intensely boiling water, binding fire and boiling liquid in the same punitive scene as the section's hot-food senses.
luna: Like the section's meat preparations, this Garden scene offers «لَحْمِ طَيْرٍ مِّمَّا يَشْتَهُونَ»; it supplies a positive food counterpart without claiming the birds are cooked.

luna: The section's duha heat and cooking-fire images have a punitive counterpart in «سَمُومٍ وَحَمِيمٍ», scorching wind and boiling water. | terra: Scorching wind and boiling water replace the gentle warmth and meal heard in the forenoon with lethal heat and drink.

luna: The next ayah gives the punished a shade of black smoke, extending the hot scene into a shade that offers no relief. | terra: The shadow is made of black smoke, converting the shelter associated with relief from sun into a product of fire.

luna: This continuation says that shade is «لَا بَارِدٍ وَلَا كَرِيمٍ», explicitly withholding cooling or comfort against the section's bodily warmth and food. | terra: The smoky shade is neither cool nor pleasant, expressly denying the two qualities a sheltering shade should give.

luna: Where the section evokes cooked food and a morning meal, this passage makes the denied ones eat from Zaqqum («لَآكِلُونَ مِن شَجَرٍ مِّن زَقُّومٍ»), an explicitly punitive food. | terra: Eating from the tree of zaqqum begins another explicit punitive meal in a passage saturated with boiling heat.

luna: This continuation says they fill their bellies from it; the section's meal against poor nutrition becomes its bodily opposite. | terra: Filling bellies from zaqqum specifies the bodily destination of the meal rather than invoking fire only in general.

luna: The next step is drinking boiling water («مِنَ الْحَمِيمِ») over the Zaqqum, extending the cooked-food scene into a painful drink. | terra: Drinking boiling water after the food supplies the meal's searing liquid counterpart.

luna: The passage says they drink like thirsty camels («شُرْبَ الْهِيمِ»); this sharpens the contrast with the section's Garden assurance of no thirst in 20:119. | terra: Drinking like desperately thirsty camels turns the source-section camel meal into a grim reversal in which camel thirst describes the diners.

luna: After the Zaqqum and boiling drink in 56:52–55, «هَٰذَا نُزُلُهُمْ» calls this their reception on Judgment Day, a pointed reversal of a welcoming meal. | terra: Calling the sequence their “hospitality” on the Day of Judgment makes the whole passage a deliberate inversion of a nourishing table.

luna: The section's B004/B002 fire meanings include cooking and burning; «النَّارَ الَّتِي تُورُونَ» asks about the fire people kindle, a direct human-use counterpart. | terra: The question about the fire people kindle places ordinary, deliberately kindled fire before the reader, the agent behind the section's frying and boiling senses.

luna: This continuation asks who produced the fire's tree («شَجَرَتَهَا»); the section's B006 also names ash from burned plants, connecting fire to plant matter. | terra: This ayah asks whether people produced the fire's tree or God did, paralleling 36:80 and grounding the section's plant-to-fire image in divine provision.

luna: This ayah calls that fire «مَتَاعًا لِلْمُقْوِينَ», provision for travelers; it makes the kindled fire useful, a boundary to the section's harmful-fire senses. | terra: The kindled fire is called a reminder and a provision for travelers, giving useful fire a food-and-sustenance setting rather than leaving it only as punishment.
terra: Vegetation delights its growers, then yellows and becomes debris; it offers another indirect living-plant-to-residue parallel, but no fire or ash is named.
terra: A Fire fueled by people and stones repeats the conjunction of bodies, fire, and stone behind the source-section hot-stone and fire-on-flesh images, though no meal is present.
terra: The garden owners swear to harvest early in the morning, beginning a morning food scene whose intended exclusion of the poor is stated in 68:24.
terra: Their morning call to one another keeps the denial of food in a deliberately early-day setting, a dark counterpart to the forenoon meal.

luna: The section's table faces poor nutrition; the garden owners secretly bar «مِسْكِينٌ» from their harvest, a concrete withholding of food from the needy. | terra: They conspire that no poor person should enter the garden that day, directly opposing the section's meal set against deprivation.

luna: After 68:24's ban on the needy, the owners go early with firm intent («وَغَدَوْا عَلَىٰ حَرْدٍ قَادِرِينَ»); this adds the planned nature of withholding the harvest. | terra: The garden owners go out early determined and believing themselves able to bar others, turning the morning harvest into a deliberate act of deprivation against the poor named in 68:24.
luna: After their exclusion plan in 68:25, the owners see the ruined orchard and say they must be mistaken; the scene shows the food source itself has disappeared.

luna: After seeing it in 68:26, they say «بَلْ نَحْنُ مَحْرُومُونَ»; their plan to exclude the poor turns into their own deprivation. | terra: When the garden is lost they confess that they themselves have been deprived, reversing their planned deprivation of the poor back upon them.
terra: The command to burn the offender in Hell belongs to the same indictment that says in 69:34 he did not urge feeding the poor, joining punitive fire to a withheld meal.

luna: The section sets the forenoon meal against undernourishment; this person «لَا يَحُضُّ عَلَىٰ طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ», refusing to urge food for the poor. | terra: The condemned person did not urge feeding the poor; the same passage then replaces the withheld meal with the eater's own repellent food in 69:36-37.

luna: The passage then says there is no food but «غِسْلِينٍ», a painful anti-meal that reverses the section's food as sustenance. | terra: The punishment offers no food except ghislīn, turning refusal to feed the poor in 69:34 into a corrupt punitive table.

luna: The next ayah says only sinners eat that food («لَا يَأْكُلُهُ إِلَّا الْخَاطِئُونَ»), identifying the opposite eater in 69:36. | terra: Only the sinners eat that food, identifying the diners at the inverted table created by 69:34 and 69:36.
terra: The blaze is named as an inescapable fire before 70:16 specifies its action upon the body.
terra: The blaze strips away the skin or extremities, directly showing fire overpowering flesh as in the source-section culinary qahr expression.
terra: “Food that chokes” and painful punishment make the meal itself unfit and harmful, another specific Quranic reversal of nourishing provision.

luna: The section's B006 qily is plant ash used to wash clothes; «وَثِيَابَكَ فَطَهِّرْ» shares the concrete act of cleansing garments, though the ayah gives no ash method. | terra: “Purify your garments” meets the source-section qily definition at its stated use: an ash preparation with which clothes are washed.
terra: The promise to cast the offender into Saqar supplies the fire destination whose later confession includes failure to feed the poor in 74:44.
terra: Saqar is described as scorching the human skin, a concise bodily realization of the source-section qahr image of fire seizing meat.

luna: The section's meal provision for the needy is reversed by the speakers' confession «لَمْ نَكُ نُطْعِمُ الْمِسْكِينَ». | terra: “We did not feed the poor” is one of the inhabitants' own reasons for reaching Saqar, directly binding withheld nourishment to the surah's fire imagery.

luna: This verse gives food to «مِسْكِينًا وَيَتِيمًا وَأَسِيرًا»; it makes the section's forenoon table a meal shared with the vulnerable, including the orphan named in its prohibition. | terra: The righteous feed food, despite loving or needing it, to the poor person, orphan, and captive; this directly realizes the section's nourishing table for the vulnerable orphan.
luna: The neighboring ayah explains the feeding in 76:8 as for God's face, seeking no reward or thanks; it adds the giver's stance to the shared meal scene.
terra: Because of the conduct exemplified by feeding the vulnerable in 76:8, God protects the righteous from the day's evil; 76:13 then specifies their Garden freedom from sun and bitter cold.

luna: The section recalls Adam's protection from duha heat; in this Garden scene people see neither sun nor severe cold («لَا يَرَوْنَ فِيهَا شَمْسًا»), extending the protection from exposure. | terra: The feeders of 76:8 are rewarded in the Garden where they see neither sun nor bitter cold, directly paralleling Adam's protection from sun exposure in 20:119.
terra: Near shade and lowered fruit join shelter from the sun to readily available food, making visible both sides of the section's forenoon image.
terra: The condemned are sent toward a three-branched “shade,” setting up a counterfeit shelter whose failure against flame is stated in 77:31.
terra: That smoke is neither shading nor protective from the flame, reversing the genuine protection from heat in 16:81 and the Garden promise in 20:119.
terra: The inhabitants taste neither coolness nor drink, reversing both relief from heat and the thirst protection promised to Adam.
terra: Only boiling water and foul fluid answer the absence of drink in 78:24, turning provision into burning harm.
terra: After the night is darkened, وَأَخْرَجَ ضُحَىٰهَا says that God brings out the earth's forenoon brightness; this is the same night-to-ḍuḥā emergence staged in surah 93.
terra: The Last Hour will seem no longer than an evening or its ضُحى; the root here measures a day's brief span, adding transience to the section's warm forenoon.
terra: The command that a human being look at his food opens a provision sequence that includes the grain named in the source-section qaly definition.
terra: God causes grain to grow from the split earth; grain is explicitly the other food the source-section says can be fried by qaly.
terra: The trench is identified as a fire abundantly supplied with fuel in the passage about believers subjected to it, giving the fire-on-human-flesh image a deliberate human setting.
terra: God brings forth green pasture, supplying the living green vegetation that the source-section qily definition says is burned; the ayah itself does not mention burning.
terra: The pasture becomes dark stubble, resembling the dark residue of the source-section plant ash, though this ayah does not identify the process as fire.
terra: In the greatest fire the condemned person neither dies nor lives, making heat suspend the ordinary boundary of bodily life rather than simply cooking or consuming flesh.

luna: The section's noon sun and cooking fire carry warmth; this passage begins with faces in «نَارًا حَامِيَةً», turning heat into punishment. | terra: Entering a fiercely hot fire begins a passage in which heat, boiling drink, and failed nourishment are made one punishment, reversing the section's warm morning table.

luna: The next ayah gives them drink from «عَيْنٍ آنِيَةٍ», a boiling spring; it continues the burning scene with scalding liquid. | terra: Drink from a boiling spring adds scalding liquid to the fire of 88:4 and the unnourishing food of 88:6-7.

luna: After the boiling spring, this ayah says there is no food except a thorny plant; it reverses the section's nourishing meal. | terra: The diners have no food except thorny growth, a concrete table of bad nourishment set within the passage's fire and boiling heat.

luna: The next ayah specifies that the thorny food neither nourishes nor relieves hunger, an exact counterpart to the section's meal against poor nutrition. | terra: لَا يُسْمِنُ وَلَا يُغْنِى مِن جُوعٍ explicitly defines that food as neither nourishing nor relieving hunger, the clearest Quranic counterpart to the section's “bad nourishment.”

luna: The section forbids overpowering the orphan; «لَا تُكْرِمُونَ الْيَتِيمَ» names the opposite failure to honor that same vulnerable person. | terra: The rebuke “you do not honor the orphan” supplies the social opposite of 93:9 and leads immediately to the failure to feed in 89:18.

luna: The next ayah says they do not urge feeding the poor («طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ»), reversing the section's meal and its care for the orphan. | terra: Failure to urge one another to feed the poor directly opposes the forenoon table and completes the orphan-and-food pair begun in 89:17.
terra: The people consume inheritance with voracious consumption immediately after neglecting the orphan and poor, contrasting self-directed devouring with withheld nourishment.
terra: After rebuking failure to honor the orphan and feed the poor, the passage has Hell brought into view; neglected nourishment and fire thus meet as cause and consequence.

luna: The section's B003 forenoon food stands against want; «إِطْعَامٌ فِي يَوْمٍ ذِي مَسْغَبَةٍ» names feeding on a day of hunger, making that contrast concrete. | terra: Feeding on a day of severe hunger is the Quran's direct answer to the section's forenoon table standing against bad nourishment.

luna: The hungry-day feeding of 90:14 is for «يَتِيمًا ذَا مَقْرَبَةٍ»; this ayah identifies the orphan, the person the section says must not be overpowered, as a meal's recipient. | terra: The first named recipient of that famine-day meal is a related orphan, directly joining the section's table to its command not to overpower the orphan.

luna: Continuing 90:14's feeding scene, this ayah names «مِسْكِينًا ذَا مَتْرَبَةٍ», a second recipient whose destitution sharpens the section's meal-versus-poor-nutrition image. | terra: This ayah adds the destitute person lying in dust to the orphan of 90:15, completing the concrete company at the hunger-day table.
terra: The same surah that defines the steep path through feeding an orphan and destitute person ends with fire closed over the rejecters, setting table and enclosing fire on opposite outcomes.

luna: The section says duha is sunlight as well as heat; the oath «وَالشَّمْسِ وَضُحَاهَا» directly joins the sun to its forenoon brightness. | terra: وَٱلشَّمْسِ وَضُحَىٰهَا attributes ḍuḥā to the sun itself, directly joining the section's oath-word to solar light and heat.
terra: The day is sworn by as it displays the sun, continuing 91:1's sun and its ḍuḥā with the full daylight manifestation of that brightness.
terra: The night covers the sun after the day displays it, paralleling the forenoon-and-stilled-night pair that opens surah 93.
terra: The warning of a blazing fire establishes the fire from which the charitable giver of 92:18 is kept away in 92:17.
terra: The deeply mindful person is kept away from the blaze, excluding fire from the giver whose defining act follows in 92:18.
terra: Giving wealth for purification identifies the human act paired with escape from fire in 92:17, a thematic counterpart to feeding the vulnerable rather than subjecting them to want.
terra: The kindled fire of God identifies the agent whose penetration into the body is completed in 104:7.
terra: The fire rises over the hearts, carrying the section's fire-taking-flesh image from the outer body to its interior.

luna: The section's meal stands against undernourishment; this verse says the Lord of the House fed Quraysh «مِّن جُوعٍ» and secured them from fear, a concrete provision parallel. | terra: God “fed them against hunger” states in compact form the provision that the section's forenoon meal sets against malnutrition.

luna: The section says not to oppress the orphan; «يَدُعُّ الْيَتِيمَ» depicts the opposing act of driving an orphan away. | terra: Harshly driving away the orphan is a concrete enactment of the qahr forbidden in 93:9 and is paired with refusal of poor feeding in the next ayah.

luna: The next ayah says he does not urge feeding the poor («طَعَامِ الْمِسْكِينِ»), a direct negation of the section's meal-for-need image. | terra: Not urging the feeding of the poor completes 107:2's orphan oppression with the bad nourishment heard by the section in the عيل family.
